Without the body, the I would not exist, and neither would human beings or words. But without the I and without words—without discourse, without logos—there would likewise be no human being, only a speechless animal.
When the body dies, the human being disappears completely and for good.
This does not mean that a human being is born simply when the body is born. A human being is also born when the I becomes capable of speaking and of understanding what is said.

So although a human being is not a purely material thing, he is immediately connected with a material thing—his body—and cannot exist without it. Purely ideal “things,” such as the concept of “table,” are connected with material things, such as actual tables, only through the mediation of human beings.
We might therefore say that concreteness passes, so to speak, from matter into the human being but does not extend as far as ideal “things,” which remain abstract.

We can consequently call not only material things but human beings concrete. Although I am not purely material, I am nevertheless, as a human being—and in particular as my own embodied self—just as concrete as any other material thing.

Now that we have defined the concept of the concrete, we can try to show why complete knowledge of any concrete phenomenon or being necessarily amounts to perfect knowledge—that is, knowledge of everything that exists.
Let us begin with a purely material, concrete thing and return to the example of the table on which I am writing now.
I will not dwell on the familiar fact that every concrete, “individual” thing possesses an enormous and almost countless variety of qualities.

It was noticed long ago that we cannot reproduce all this richness in words. Whole libraries could be written about my table and still leave out qualities that would remain to be described. One need only think of all the subtle shades of colour it contains.
Perhaps it is false to say, as people often do, that a concrete object possesses an infinite number of qualities. But the number is certainly so large that in practice we could never exhaust it.
In principle, however, I might know every quality that belongs to my table and to my table alone without knowing anything about other things.
Even then, though, I would still not know everything that can be known—or said—about it.

There is another whole class of characteristics, some belonging to it alone and some shared with other things. To know everything there is to know about my table, I must know these characteristics too, which means that I must also know the other things that share them.
My table, for example, has to be somewhere.
There might conceivably be another table somewhere in an empty corner of space. But that table plainly would not be my table, the desk at which I am writing now.
This table stands in a particular room, furnished in a particular way. To know the table completely, I therefore also have to know the room in which it stands.
We can perfectly well imagine another desk that, considered entirely by itself, is indistinguishable from mine. But if that desk is in another room, then it is obviously not mine.
So one of the facts that determines this desk as my desk is that it stands in this particular room. And that determination includes knowledge of the room itself.

Imagine, for example, that while I am away I ask someone to move my desk somewhere else. I have to describe the desk to that person. But if I forget to say where it is—if I do not specify the room in which it stands—he will not find it. In that sense, he will not know which desk I mean.

And even if I tell him, “Take the desk in such-and-such a room,” there may be two desks in that room. Once again, he will not know which one is mine—not to mention the possibility that someone may have replaced my desk with another table.
So for him to know my desk well enough, he must know which desk it is and where it is, including the room in which it stands.
But what is true of the table is also true of the room.

The room too is somewhere. To find it, and therefore to know which room it is, we have to know the building that contains it. To know the building, we must also know the street, the city, the country—Moscow, after all, can be found both in the USSR and in the United States—and, if necessary, the continent.
In other words, we eventually have to know where on Earth my table is.
Of course, if the practical task is simply to move my desk, there is little point in specifying that it is on planet Earth, since at present there is no interplanetary transport.
But the fact that the table is on Earth unquestionably forms part of our knowledge of it.

There is nothing inconceivable about another table somewhere in the universe that, taken by itself, is indistinguishable from my desk. Knowing that mine is on Earth, and knowing where Earth itself is, ultimately means knowing the universe as a whole.
That is one side of the matter.
On the other hand, if I want to know what my desk is, I also have to know what it is made of.
Wood consists of chemical elements, which form molecules, which in turn consist of atoms, which consist of electrons, and so on.
So from one direction, complete knowledge of my table presupposes knowledge of the universe as a whole. From another, it presupposes knowledge of the atomic world.
In other words, I know my table completely, and can answer every possible question about it, only if I know everything that can be known about the material world in general.
And I must know that world not only across space but also through time.

I have to know the “history” of my desk and of the material from which it was made. I must know the history of the wood from which its boards were cut. And I must know that history all the way back to the beginning—to the “beginning of time.”
My table is determined not only by the fact that it stands in a particular room. Its existence is also determined by the fact that it belongs to me, that I write on it, and so on.
And even after knowing all this, I still do not know it completely.
To do that, I would also have to know who I am.
Complete knowledge of my desk therefore necessarily includes not only complete knowledge of the material world but also complete knowledge of myself.

And if complete knowledge of myself includes—as we will now see—every form of knowledge that is possible at all, then complete knowledge of my table really is nothing other than perfect knowledge: knowledge of everything whatsoever.
What is true of my desk is equally true of every other concrete—that is, real and material—thing.

The reason I cannot know my desk completely without also knowing the whole universe is that every real, material thing is actually connected with the entire material world and is in fact inseparable from it.
Someone once expressed this very vividly by saying that the match I strike has an effect even on the Sun.
Every real thing interacts with all the others, and together they form a single whole. Strictly speaking, only this whole is fully real.
I can detach one part of it from another only in my imagination.

My desk is really contained within the universe, and the real universe really contains my desk. A universe without this desk “exists” only in my imagination. It is an “abstraction,” because the real, concrete, material universe in fact includes the desk.

Conversely, my desk is real, material, and concrete only insofar as it forms part of the universe that actually exists. Outside that universe my desk too would be merely an “abstraction,” something that “exists” only in my imagination, because in fact it exists only within the universe.

It is precisely because a concrete thing is inseparable in reality from the whole of the rest of the real world that complete and concrete knowledge of any real thing becomes perfect, “absolute,” or universal knowledge.
As someone rightly observed, complete knowledge of even the smallest blade of grass would necessarily give us complete knowledge of the structure of the universe as a whole.
But people usually forgot something here.
The real universe contains not only every real and material thing but also every person who actually lives within it, together with their consciousness, knowledge, thoughts, speech, and so on.
If my desk outside my room is an abstraction, then a desk without my body sitting beside it is just as much an abstraction.
And this body contains my I, which not only allows the body to put its weight on the desk but also allows it to write definite and meaningful words on it.
All of this plainly forms part of the concrete reality of my desk—and of the universe.
More generally, since the only things we know are things we actually know, the thing we know is not simply a material “thing.” It is also a thing known by me.
A “thing without my knowledge of it” is an abstraction in exactly the same sense as a “thing outside the universe.”
We should emphasize once again, however, that this is true only when we are dealing either with a concrete thing—that is, a real or material thing—or with a concrete human being.

When we are dealing with an ideal “thing,” meaning something abstract and non-material, it is perfectly possible to know everything that can be known about it without knowing anything definite about other things, whether ideal or real.

We can see this simply by remembering that it is possible, for example, to know all the geometrical properties of a triangle without knowing algebra, Russian, the structure of the atom, or the structure of the universe.

The same is true of the properties of the “table in general.” We can know the word, concept, or idea of “table” without knowing anything about particular people, particular tables, the universe, and so on.
Only complete and concrete knowledge of concrete things or human beings therefore necessarily becomes universal or perfect knowledge.
The example of my desk has shown that this is true of concrete things. We can now see, by taking myself as the example, that it is equally true of concrete human beings.
If I want to give an exhaustive answer to the concrete question “Who am I?”, then among other things I must say that I am this person who is, at this moment, sitting at his desk and writing.
So my knowledge of myself must include knowledge of the table—and therefore, as we have just seen, knowledge of the material universe as a whole, including my body.
But I must also speak about my I and its contents.
Those contents are my thoughts—that is, meaningful words or concepts, ideas.
And it is easy to see that complete knowledge of the contents that make up my I includes knowledge of the entire ideal world.
For what I do not know—mathematics or Greek, for example—characterizes me just as much as what I do know.
And to know what I do not know, one would have to know the whole ideal world.
Complete, concrete knowledge of one concrete human being therefore includes complete knowledge of both the real world and the ideal world.
It also includes complete knowledge of that person’s human I, which forms the point of connection between those two worlds.
It is easy to see that such knowledge is nothing other than complete knowledge of the entire human or historical world from the “beginning of time” down to the present moment.
My I is characterized, among other things, by the fact that I am writing now—that is, that I am translating concepts from ideal existence into real existence, turning them into marks on paper.
And I am writing precisely what I am, in fact, writing.
But I could not write what I am writing if I had not read Hegel.
Hegel, in turn, could not have written what he wrote if he had not read Kant, and so on.
And the “first” philosopher could not have philosophized unless he had already been able to speak.
So once again we have to trace the path back from the “first” philosopher to the “first” human being who began to speak.

That human being appeared on Earth when, “for the first time,” certain animals began to speak—why they did so we will learn later. In other words, we have to go all the way back to the “first” human being as such.
To know completely what my concrete human I is, I therefore have to know its historical past from the “first” human being down to this very moment when the questions about it are being answered.
Every complete form of knowledge concerning any concrete thing or concrete human being is therefore perfect or absolute knowledge.
Let us now use another example to show that universal knowledge of oneself also includes the kind of knowledge normally called “philosophical” or “metaphysical.”
One only has to start answering almost any concrete question about oneself before the answers very quickly become “metaphysical.”
If I answer, “Because I like it and it gives me pleasure,” then the chain of questions comes to an abrupt end.
But by answering in this way, I am effectively admitting that I do not know why I wash—in other words, that I do not fully know who I am.
And in all honesty I cannot say that I particularly enjoy washing. When the water is cold, it can be positively unpleasant, yet I wash anyway.
